bank_access: Realistic: Canadian banks open non-resident accounts in person, electronically or by phone; some (Scotiabank) start online, but a charity's corporate account typically needs at least one in-person branch visit by a signatory for KYC.

Needs a local visit: US banks require in-person branch KYC with passport/visa and an IRS EIN; many also demand a physical US address, so a remote founder needs an in-person signatory trip or local agent.
Effectively blocked: no independent charity sector exists, and banks serve residents/authorized state entities; even personal MLC accounts require temporary residence permits, not tourist status.
Needs a local visit: banks (NCB, CIBC) open non-resident accounts, but non-residents must be physically present at a branch with passport plus a second ID; no fully remote onboarding.
Needs a local visit: Bahamian banks open non-resident accounts under central-bank FATF KYC guidance, but the applicant must appear in person for identity verification; remote opening is rare.
Needs a local visit: banks accept non-resident accounts, but non-residents must be present for account opening (CIBC rule); online application only pre-fills the branch completion.
Needs a local visit: non-residents must appear at a branch (First Citizens, Republic Bank) with passport, three-month utility bill or lease as address proof; no remote opening.
Needs a local visit: banks (Trium, A&B Bank) accept non-resident and corporate accounts with enhanced due diligence, but an in-person branch visit by the signatory is the standard route.
Needs a local visit: banks (Grenada Co-op, Republic Bank) accept non-national accounts with two IDs, but the applicant/signatory must appear in person at a branch; no fully remote route.

Needs a local visit plus enhanced AML diligence: banks apply enhanced due diligence to non-residents (purpose, expected transactions); in-person branch appearance is standard for individual and corporate accounts.
Needs a local visit: CIBC and others open non-resident accounts, but non-residents must be physically present with two forms of ID; Bank of St. Lucia runs a dedicated non-national onboarding path.
Needs a local visit: banks (BOVSG, Republic) accept non-resident accounts with overseas addresses, but in-person branch appearance by the signatory is standard; offshore desks may be more flexible.
Needs a local visit, easiest of the Caribbean: the FSU requires no local connection; non-resident individual and corporate accounts are accepted with source-of-funds documentation, in person.
Needs a local visit: major banks (Popular, BHD, Santa Cruz) open non-resident accounts with a valid passport, often without address proof; corporate accounts still need an in-person director visit.
Needs a local visit: per US trade guidance, foreigners can open USD/HTG accounts immediately with passport and a minimum deposit, but the process is in person in Port-au-Prince; no remote KYC.
Needs a local visit: banks (Scotiabank, BBVA) open non-resident accounts with passport, migratory document and SAT RUT; in-person branch visits are the norm and fully remote opening is rare.

Needs a local visit plus RUT: banks require in-person appearance and an active RUT (tax registration, obtainable by foreigners); passport-only accounts are often restricted to legal residents (e.g. BAM).

Needs a local visit: the central bank delegated non-resident account authority to domestic banks (Atlantic, Caye International), which accept non-residents with low minimums; in-person branch visits standard.
Needs a local visit: major banks (Banco Agrícola, Cuscatlán) accept foreigners; a passport may open a basic savings account, but full access typically needs a Salvadoran NIT and in-person KYC.
Needs a local visit: banks require the applicant to appear with passport, residency/visa proof and an NIT (tax registration); a remote founder would need a local agent or an in-person trip.
